answer:
Train a router on the incremental quality benefit of the stronger model, not on prompt length alone. Features can include task type, language, context length, retrieval confidence, requested tools, and calibrated uncertainty. Define a cost-quality objective and segment-specific quality floors; safety-sensitive tasks may have fixed routing policies rather than learned thresholds.

Start with offline paired evaluations of small and large model outputs on representative traffic. Choose routing thresholds on a separate validation set and retain randomized exploration traffic to detect blind spots. A small-model answer can trigger escalation before any output is released; midstream switching must restart explicitly rather than concatenate different answers.

Version routers with the model pair and pricing assumptions. Enforce tenant budgets, deadlines, fallback rules, and overload behavior independently of the router. Measure quality by segment, escalation rate, latency, tokens, and cost per successful task. There is no per-request quality guarantee from a classifier: report statistical bounds on held-out/online measurements and detect changes in traffic or model capabilities that invalidate calibration.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Choose the stronger model when estimated incremental utility exceeds incremental cost: $\mathbb E[\Delta U|x]>\lambda\Delta C$, subject to hard quality/latency constraints. Calibrate on representative paired outcomes and track routing regret against stronger-model performance. A cheap router that systematically misses rare difficult cases can erase the apparent savings through downstream failures. [3](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://lmsys.org/blog/2024-07-01-routellm/) and [2](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents).
